newsitem.title: USA: USDA says no Mexican ban on U.S. sorghum imports.
newsitem.headline: USDA says no Mexican ban on U.S. sorghum imports.

text.p: No restrictions are being put in place by Mexico on U.S. sorghum imports, a U.S. Agriculture Department official said Friday, however imports will likely start off sluggish in 1997 due to Mexico's own large crop.
There had been rumours Mexico had cancelled phytosanitary permits for incoming U.S. sorghum.
The USDA official, who asked not to be identified, acknowledged there had been conflicting signals across the border but said: "There is no import ban being put in place."
He pointed to the fact Mexico has released 70 percent of the calendar year 1997 import tariff rate quotas.

"But you would expect, especially given the size of the crop that they're harvesting, that the first quarter 1997 would be a really low import period for sorghum anyway," the USDA official added. "They're flush with it. They're flush with corn also which competes with sorghum in their feed sector."
Mexico and Japan are the top customers for U.S. sorghum.
USDA projects Mexico will import 2.5 million tonnes of sorghum in 1996/97, up from 1.8 million tonnes in 1995/96.
Most of the grain will likely come from the United States, which has harvested a mammoth 820 million bushels of sorghum, pushing prices down.

The USDA official said the sales pace would have to pick up later on if the U.S. was to meet its import forecast because there was not that much on the books at the moment for delivery in the first quarter of 1997.
